p: Yeah. A lot of it’s going in-house. We do still have a marketing budget and we are– we do buy specific ads through LinkedIn or paid LinkedIn posts, I guess, to reach out to a larger audience. And I think specifically– I’ll have to get back to you about the multiple languages, but that’s– we appreciate that way. I think that’s a great idea.

Okay. No, only because just for my former work in the nonprofit sector, the language is very important and key, and I know that there’s a lot of– you know, for example even local media that a lot of folks pay attention to and may spread the word through their friends and family networks that way to say, hey, there’s this program out there. So, just wanted to put that out there.
Yeah, that's great. Thank you.

May 2024 report titled New York City Small Business Recovery, Patterns of Growth in a Changing Economy showed that at the time New York State had over 183,000 small businesses, more than ever before, and showed substantial recovery from the drops seen during COVID. And over the last two years economies have changed drastically on the local, national, and global levels. And so do you track the number of small businesses located in the city? If not, is that something that the corporation is willing to track and if yes, what is the current number of small businesses and what are the trends that you’re seeing.

I’ll have to get back to you if we track those small businesses, and if we don’t, we can look into tracking them. We do work very closely with SBS as well as we are very focused on small business. They're sort of the backbone of the economy here, and they are good, you know, paying jobs for people. And we– what we do is– we have programs to promote small business and support small businesses, but we also use our assets to tenant out for small businesses, specifically – for example, Brooklyn Army Terminal [sic], many of those small business or manufacturing and industrial companies, and we are very focused on ensuring that we provide them tenant space.
Great. And just my last questions around revenue. Do you conduct any analysis on the efficacy of incentive programs like RACE and REAP on tax revenue for the city?

We do track, I think the usage– I have to get back to you exactly, but we do track on sort of– like, we look backwards and see like how many companies use RACE or REAP, where they– what those companies were to see if people are using it and what they’re using it for, and where it’s like

successful or not. Yes, we have a strategy group that does all that analysis.
Okay. And have you considered expanding existing marketing, business attraction for these programs?

So, we were involved in sort of advising City Hall on sort of potential incentive programs and so we’ll continue to play that role. We haven't done it like recently, but we continue to play that role with City Hall.
Okay. And then do the businesses tend to be smaller, larger in size that benefit from REAP and RACE?
I think it’s smaller to medium.
Smaller to medium, okay.
But I think it’s on a case by case basis.
Okay. And the main city-funded subsidy, for example, for Amazon HQ2 was the REAP program and it would have cost the city up to $1.4 billion in tax subsidy.
Yeah, that’s the exception.

Yeah. Since REAP is an as-of-right program, the city would not have had the authority to limit or condition the use of this tax break by Amazon or any other large company. So, does EDC think an open-ended tax break like that is wise use? Are you looking into that or any of the other programs?

Again, I think we provide the statistics and look at it. We– and we offer that up. It’s not in our sort of decision-making power to decide on that, but we do analyze it and provide– you know, as you know, we have IDA which is a discretionary tax incentive program, and so we really– we really look at those very specifically and analyze those to see that it’s making sense for the communities in the city.
No, that’s great. I love data. So, anything you guys have to inform that–
[interposing] Yeah.
would be wonderful.
We’d be happy to share, and I’ll get back to you on the size of the companies, but I might have– I’m not really sure. I think it varies.
Okay. Perfect. Chair Maloney, I’m passing it over to you.

Thank you so much, Chair Lee. Thank you for your testimony and for the work that you have been carrying forward over the past several months. We spoke about some of the economic trends and the import of investment in programs like RACE and REAP that are helping to bring businesses and keep employers here in New York. How are you looking at market uncertainty and thinking about new programs in this economic environment to address some of the concerns that Speaker Menin raised about creating jobs here in New York?

Yeah. I think– you know, as I said, we have a group that looks at I see how effective they are, and again, who’s using it, like where they’re going, etcetera. What types of industries– and so we can provide as a resource. We don’t make the policy decisions on these as-of-right incentives. And we focus on the IDA benefits that we

provide for the discretionary benefits that are significant and meaningful.
So, with the savings of $2.1 million, that’s directed just at the marketing. The actual programs are not expected to be decreased?
Correct.

Great. And just having been an EDC alum can’t overstate how important it is to have those intentional strategy investments and programs that are trying to create jobs here in New York. I appreciate hearing about everything you’ve been doing and especially over the past couple of months as the interim president, but wanted to at least touch on the fact that we don’t have a permanent president in EDC. In December of last year, the former CEO and President Kimball [sic] announced he was going to be departing. We’re now almost at June, six months, and I’m wondering– I know, I have a full confidence in the abilities of the acting leadership, but as we’re talking about long-term economic growth, how are you to plan for those multi-year conversations without the formal authority of being deemed the president.

Yeah. Thank you. We appreciate that question. Yes, it’s been a few months now, and it’s really been a privilege of a lifetime. I did not expect to serve this role, and it’s been a tremendous experience. I’ve had a real– it’s been a real pleasure, and it’s been a great experience for me to work with all the EDC teams. As you know, it’s an incredibly talented group of individuals that have such enormous specialities in such a diverse number of areas. I’ve also really been able to work closely with Deputy Mayor Julie Su and her team, as well as the mayor. So, we really have not stopped. We have completely moved forward not only in the sort of of everyday work of managing 224 assets and 60 million square feet and all of the programs that we do have in terms of innovation industries and workforce development and our whole capital team, NYC ferries– I mean, I could go on and on and on. The economic monthly snapshot– but we are– have also done a tremendous amount for the mayor’s new initiatives such as the modular bathrooms and NYC Groceries which is an incredible, incredible initiative that really has pulled together all the– everything great about EDC, between real estate

transactions to strategy to asset management. And yeah, so it’s– we haven’t stopped. We continue to move forward and we continue– and ultimately, the President is the Mayor’s decision, and so we look forward to his decision.
Have you received a timeline, or an update–
[interposing] I have not.
on where we are with filling–
[interposing] No, I have not.
vacant role? No?
It’s all business. We just do business.
And how regularly are you receiving direction from Deputy Mayor Su or from the administration?

Oh, we work very closely with Deputy Mayor Su. We’re constantly working with her multiple times a week. We have meetings and ongoing conversations. And then the Mayor has also been very involved in the NYC Grocery stores initiative, so we work with him directly as well.
Do you have any sense of the causes for delays?
No.
And is it impacting day-to-day morale at all in EDC’s offices?

No. I think, again, it’s an incredibly special group of people that are really committed to the mission of what they’re doing, and so they stay– everyone’s staying focused and really trying to move. In fact, you know, everyone’s so passionate about what they’re working on that it’s– they just continue moving forward at the speed that they have normally done.
Well, we’re all eager to see this position filled, but you also seem great.
Thank you.

I want to move onto what was already mentioned, the city-backed insurance. On the expense side, this is the biggest shift from the Prelim Budget ot now, and I’m encouraged by– I’ve got it actually printed out, the Block by Block Plan, and you know, housing affordability is a top priority of the Council, as

well. So, I appreciate the effort to address one of the highest costs which is an insurance. When we’re talking about the criteria for which homes are going to receive insurance– city-backed insurance through the program, what’s the selection criteria?

Yeah, thank you. That’s an important question. We thought about this a lot. It’s sort of– if you look at the pool of affordable homes where there are new affordable homes or existing stock, we didn’t want to have the best performing, so to speak, and we didn’t want to be the intro of last resort. We want to sort of take the middle block. So,let’s call it the middle 60 percent. That's– that is where we’re– that’s the stock that we will be insuring. And so HPD will be looking at their portfolio and sort of their pipeline for bringing affordable housing, and they’ll direct us in terms of what– but that’s the criteria. It’s sort of the middle group.
And so how will limiting participation to that kind of subset of owners impact the overall risk pool?

So, that’s why we’re picking that sort of middle selection, because we’re

not taking on any extra risk. What we’re doing is we’re offering this lower cost, because we’re not having the overhead and the profit and the cost of capital that the insurance companies have. So it’s not about taking on more risk or liability. It’s just about doing it more efficiently because the city doesn’t have the same situation as these private insurers.

The report, and you mentioned this before, how we hope that this is going to reverse cost trends and then ultimately subsidize the insurance program. I’m just wondering if you could speak a little bit more to how this will reverse cost trends.

So, we’re hoping that this sort of sets a standard and becomes in– what we’re really hoping is that it’s going to be able to leverage other investors to be part of this insurance solution. And also, we’re– we expect that it’s going to help reduce the subsidy needed to bring on HPD housing which will allow us to bring more housing. So, for example, about $500 and $700 million savings brings about an additional 2,000 units of affordable housing.

So, in the case that there were something like a Hurricane Sandy which caused billions of dollars in damage, would the city be liable for claims relating to those types of damages, or if it’s, you know, any damage related to the distress of the building? Just to understand the operations.

Yeah. Thank you for that. That’s an important question. We are going to look for the re-insurance market. This is typically what insurance providers do. They re-insure sort of certain risks, and so we’re going to tap into the re-insurance market for those, like, catastrophic sort of– we haven’t made the decision exactly, but that’s an option for us for that very reason.
The question comes at trying to secure the city from potentially as you said, having higher risk for, you know, a budget deficit down the line if an event were to happen in the city–

[interposing] Exactly, and that’s where the re-insurance market I think can be really effective, and so we’re going to be

insuring– looking into that. That’s part of the whole plan for the insurance program.
My last question on the insurance, is– the Executive Plan includes $20 million in FY27 and then $40 million following. Does that include the cost for staffing and operating the programs?
Yes, we’re going to have a third-party operator. So there’ll be a minimal cost to– for that operator. Yeah, so that’ll be included in the $100 million.
And would that operator be responsible for conducting inspections or determining risks at each of the sites that we’re–

Yeah, there’s going to be a– you know, there’s going to be an actuary who’s going to help us sort of assess the risk. So that has been procured, and then we’ll have to work out the actual agreement, but it’s not like the city or EDC is going to be assessing the risks for these housing. It’s going to be experts.

Thank you. I had one question on the five-year versus the 10-year Capital Plan that I alluded to in my opening remarks,

and then I’m going to turn to Chanel Thomas-Henry. But the five-year Capital Plan decreased over $700 million in the Executive Budget, while the 10-year plan remained unchanged. I’m wondering if you can speak to why a substantial amount of funding was extend into the out-years and if at all there are any impacts of sequencing of some of the projects that are really important that EDC manages?

Yes. Thank you. So this is a normal regular exercise that OMB has each agency do for the 10-year Capital Plan, and they need to smooth out or stretch out the capital costs each of the years. And so, those projects that were selected, either that they– they didn’t need to be in the timeline that they were, so they were able to stretch it out. Or it’s a very– it’s a very fluid capital plan. So if we need it, we can always pull that money forward. It’s not like set in stone, so it’s very flexible. But in terms of just putting out the plan, they need to just smooth it out, and they do this with all the agencies.
So, there’s no impact on–
[interposing] No.
the timeline of completion of those major projects?
No. It’s not like it’s going to delay it in any way.
Great. And also no projects are being prioritized over others or–
[interposing] No.
no shifts on that front?
No. If it’s approved, then we’re– we can sort of move it as it needs to be moved.
Thank you. I’m now turning it to Council Member Chanel Thomas-Henry.

Thank you, Chair. So, I’ve been doing a series of business tours, and I had the privilege of visiting a few cannabis businesses. So, in the Executive Budget it rolls over $7.1 million from fiscal year 2026 to fiscal 27 for the Cannabis Impact Fund, because no loans were distributed this fiscal year as the program transitioned. While I appreciate the expansion of eligibility, what specific challenges caused the delay, and what assurances can you provide

that these funds will reach businesses expeditiously in 27?

Yes. Thank you. So, we structured the cannabis loan fund into two phases. The first phase was about $1.4 million. There’s about like 200 or so businesses that had these licenses. They were sort of justice-involved individuals were the owners. And that we provided 14 loans, about 80 applied. Phase two is sort of expanding like you– and the cap on that loan was about $100,000. We’ve expanded in phase two to 540 businesses that are eligible and so far we have had about 60 apply. Again, it’s a rolling sort of application, and we’re estimating– and the cap on the size of those loans are $500,000. So, they’re higher loan amounts. We’re expecting that we’re going to be providing loans starting in the fall of this year and through like 2028. So, it’s going to be sort of an ongoing program, and about 26– we’re estimating about– projecting about 26 loans will be given out on that.

Okay. And how is EDC tracking where the dollars go geographically? Like, can you provide data on

whether communities that were most impacted by cannabis enforcements, including communities of color, specifically in Queens, Brooklyn and the Bronx–
[interposing] Yes.
are receiving a proportionate share of those dollars?
Yeah, we can provide that information for you, yeah.

Okay. The RISE program– so the Executive Budget includes additional funding for the RISE program which helps businesses adopted innovative climate-resilient technology. How is EDC ensuring that small businesses in climate-vulnerable neighborhoods like Corona and East Elmhurst in my district are aware of and able to access these resources, particularly those that may lack the capacity to navigate complex application processes? And kind of piggybacking off what Council Member Lee said, the language barrier often times.

Yes. So, this is a federally-funded program, and in the implementation of how the RISE program works, I’ll have to get back

to you on that, because I’m not familiar exactly how it’s implemented for small businesses.
Okay.
But I know it’s for small business to promote climate resilience.
Chair, if it’s okay, I do want to ask before my time expires– Council Member Epstein had to leave but had a question. Do you mind if I ask his question?
Sure, go ahead.
Innovative East– Innovation East was approved in 2025. Is EDC looking at this project to do this project at all, or?
Okay. I’m sorry, say it–
Innovation East–
[interposing] Yes.
was approved in 2025. Again, this is Council Member Epstein. Is EDC looking at that project, and are they– if you are looking at it, is it the same plan or have any alterations been made of the plan?
There’s no alterations to the plan.
But you are still looking for moving it forward?
Yes.
Thank you.
Okay. Council Member Brewer?

Thank you very much. On the insurance, I mean– may he rest in peace, Dick Ravage [sp?] and now it’s on [inaudible]. They have the Milkford [sp?] program. Why are we not just using that insurance which is supposed to be affordable housing?

I think we believe that having it be city-backed creates efficiencies that the private sector can’t create, can’t benefit from, which is the overhead and profit margin as well as the cost of capital. I think Milford did have, but it was not successful. So, we came in and came up with a solution with city capital.
Okay. I’d like to hear more about that.
Or city tax levy, sorry, not capital.

I want to hear more about that from John, but okay. The other question I have is just in terms of AI– I know you heard it about from the Speaker, but what– I mean, I’m supportive generally, but I know that the person who’s doing most is David Greenfield who has a large nonprofit working with people who are trying to get food, and he trains every single Friday. He has a massive training for his employees on AI, mandated. So, my question is what are we doing as a city to try to do something similar so that people are part of the solution and not left behind?

Yeah, I think this is something– AI is something that we are keeping a close look at. We do have at EDC some programs, probably not on the scale that would be incredibly impactful, but we do have some library programs that are educating people to get to communities through the libraries. We have AI Nexus [sic] which is helping some small businesses,you know, learn about AI and how it impacts their businesses. So, we are

doing some of that, but it’s something that we need to keep a close watch on and dynamically–
[interposing] So, you don’t have any training money to do what David Greenfield’s doing for Met Council?
We don’t have that right now.
Okay. In terms of specific issues– South Street Seaport, they need John Street lots, what are you doing about that?
Yeah, so we have a close partnership with South Street Seaport and we’re always looking to help them, you know, with any opportunities or issues that they have, so we’ll continue to work with them.
They need the lot.
Yeah, we’ll be talking to them about it. We haven’t worked with that in particular, but we have a very good relationship with them, and we constantly help them with the opportunities that they have.

Okay. And same thing with Pier 15 and Pier 19– whey do we need a

Pier 19? What’s going on with the piers in the South Street Seaport?
I’ll have to get back to you about Pier 19.
Okay. We don’t like Pier 19. We want to keep Pier 15 and Pier 16, because that helps the South Street Seaport Museum. That’s a historic area. It’s not meant to be something else.
Understood.
I’m not going to give up on the South Street Seaport Museum. It wouldn’t be there if I hadn’t fussed, and I will continue. The Bloomingdale Library, that’s your project.
Yes.
But we would like it to be– it’s on city-owned land. Why can’t it be 100 percent affordable?
So, if it’s 100 percent affordable, it would be in the HPD pipeline which–
[interposing] We’d like it to go to HPD and get it away from EDC.
So, part of the strategy of bringing housing online faster is using the mixed-income model so we can cross-subsidize.
I’m familiar with it. I’m from Manhattan.

So, and as you know, there are only certain areas where this kind of works, and this is one of those areas, and it’s important for us to bring housing stock on fast. As you know, there’s a real housing shortage, so the decision was made that this was going to be this sort of mixed–
[interposing] Okay, it’s not going to– there may be other issues that come up, so it may not happen as you think. And then–
[interposing] Understood.
you’ll at some point get back to me about my beach?

Yes. There was a study that was done in 2015, and we’re continuing to look at it. It didn’t– I think the study came back that it didn’t– we weren’t ready for it, but we’ll continue to look at it and work with you.
I want to be able to go to the water, you know that. Okay, thank you. I could go on and on, but I'll stop.

Okay. I just had a really quick question on behalf of Council Member Paladino who is watching online. Just in terms of the grocery stores, can you just– I’ll ask them all at once. And I think you actually answered some of these, but for the record I just wanted to note her questions. She was asking about the prices and what they’re going to be, which I know you said were certain percentages. And then are you going to be carrying name brands? If not, what can we expect to see on the shelves? Are people going to have the vast amount of options that we have in our grocery stores now? And I think you sort of answered that question, but if you could again just for the record.

Yeah, a lot of that’s going to be worked out when we have the third-party grocery operator, but basically it is– how we’re envisioning that it’s going to be like a regular grocery store with this core basket being discounted.
And mostly focused on fresh foods, healthy items, those types of–
[interposing] And everyday groceries.

Okay. And not going to overlap. There’s going to be items with bodegas, at bodegas that are not going to be there, and grocery store items that are not going to be in those, but they can still get elsewhere in the local supermarkets, right?
Say that again.

So, in other words, your– it’s– there’s going to be some overlap in items, but a lot of them are– because they’re mostly focused on fresh items, healthy foods, a lot of it is– you know, in other words, the local stores and bodegas are still going to be carrying things that that supermarket will not.

Yeah, so, yes. There’ll be things that were not– will not be offering in the NYC Groceries that are big in bodegas like lottery tickets, tobacco products, alcohols, things like that. But we will only be discounting a core basket and sort of– as we understand the sort of highly-profitable items for bodegas are not going to be discounted.
Okay, prefect.
I was– I used to buy live chickens at that location. I don’t want to tell you what happened to them after I purchased them, but at that location. Thank you very much.
